August 11, 2026
Public Utility Commission of Texas
1701 N. Congress Avenue
P.O. Box 13326
Austin, Texas 78711-3326
RE:  Project No. 58000, Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in the ERCOT Region; Comments of the Texas Blockchain Council
Dear Commissioners:
The Texas Blockchain Council ("TBC") respectfully submits these comments on the Commission's proposal to update wholesale and investor-owned utility retail transmission cost recovery in the ERCOT region. TBC represents more than one hundred member companies advancing blockchain and digital-asset innovation in Texas. Among our largest members are data-center and cryptocurrency-mining operators and developers whose facilities are directly affected by the Commission's proposed treatment of large loads. TBC supports fair, transparent transmission cost allocation and agrees that large-load customers should bear the costs they cause. The question is how to measure those costs without severing the connection between transmission charges and the service a customer actually receives.
TBC supports the Commission's general transition from four coincident peaks (4CP) to twelve coincident peaks (12CP). TBC is not asking the Commission or ERCOT to select different intervals, to create customer-selected peaks, or to substitute a system net-load peak for the Commission's proposed monthly system-peak intervals. The Commission and ERCOT should continue to identify the twelve monthly 30-minute coincident-peak intervals. TBC's proposal concerns only how an individual large-load customer's contribution is measured during those intervals: by settlement-quality net grid withdrawal at the customer's point of interconnection (POI). [1]
TBC separately opposes the proposed large-load minimum billing demand. Under proposed §25.193(d), the minimum would be the greatest of contracted peak demand, the customer's highest non-coincident peak (NCP) in the prior year, or its 12CP demand, and billing would begin when service is made available even if the customer has not energized or is not fully using the reserved capacity, for no less than 20 years. [1] That structure is broader than necessary to address legitimate concerns about speculative projects, stranded investment, and cost shifting. It also can neutralize the marginal transmission-price signal that makes coincident-peak pricing valuable: if a customer's billing determinant does not change when it curtails during a system peak, the rate design should not assume that the customer will continue to provide the same level of voluntary demand response and grid-supportive flexibility.
I.  TBC Supports 12CP With Settlement-Quality Net Grid Withdrawal at the Point of Interconnection
The Commission's proposal defines the ERCOT 12CP intervals as the monthly ERCOT system peak-demand interval for each of the twelve months from October through September and uses 30-minute intervals. [1] TBC supports that framework. Expanding from four summer peaks to twelve monthly peaks broadens the period over which customers are measured while preserving the core feature of coincident-peak allocation: customers remain responsible in proportion to their measured contribution when the system establishes the relevant peaks.
For each ERCOT-selected monthly 30-minute peak interval, TBC recommends that a large-load customer's billing demand be the settlement-quality net import from the transmission system at the applicable POI. The method is straightforward:
Monthly Net CP Demand = Metered Grid Import at the Point of Interconnection During the Applicable ERCOT Monthly Peak Interval
12CP Net Grid Withdrawal = Average of the Customer's Twelve Monthly Net CP Demand Values
Where the POI meter already measures net imports, the Commission need not theoretically subtract every generator, storage device, or individual load located behind the meter. It can use the amount that the customer actually withdrew from the ERCOT transmission system during the relevant interval. If a co-located generator is unavailable during a monthly peak and the customer increases its grid import, that higher withdrawal is captured automatically. The same method therefore recognizes verified self-supply when it performs and removes the credit when it does not.
The contracted-demand concept should follow the same principle. For a Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network (WLPUN), ERCOT's protocols contemplate an established MW withdrawal limit at a single POI determined through a system-wide interconnection study. [2] That enforceable withdrawal limit - not the gross internal demand of every load behind the POI - is the relevant measure of the firm transmission service the grid has committed to provide. A campus with 1,000 MW of internal demand but an enforceable 400 MW maximum grid-withdrawal limit is not receiving 1,000 MW of firm transmission service.
TBC recommends the same functional treatment for qualified BYOG arrangements, co-located generation, and energy storage. The credit should not be based merely on nameplate capacity. It should be tied to settlement-quality metering and telemetry, applicable interconnection and planning studies, operational availability, enforceable operating requirements, and a contractual or physical limitation on the customer's entitlement to withdraw above its established firm limit. Likewise, controllable and non-firm loads should not be billed as though every MW were continuously entitled to firm service when the customer has accepted enforceable curtailment or withdrawal restrictions.
II.  The Proposed 20-Year Minimum Billing Demand Should Be Rejected
The minimum billing demand is not necessary to implement 12CP. It is a separate overlay that would adjust a large load's measured 12CP upward whenever contracted peak demand or annual NCP is higher. Proposed §25.252 would also require a large-load interconnection agreement with a term of at least 20 years, while proposed §25.193 and §25.252 would cause billing to begin when transmission capacity is made available and would require 240 consecutive monthly payments during the first 20 years based on the greater of contracted peak demand, prior-year NCP, or 12CP demand. [1]
That approach can disconnect a substantial portion of the transmission bill from the customer's actual contribution during the 12 monthly peaks. A customer that invests in on-site generation, storage, automated load controls, or a WLPUN structure may reduce its actual grid withdrawal and provide measurable system value, yet receive little or no transmission-cost recognition if it remains billed at its original contracted peak. A flexible load may curtail at every monthly system peak and still see no meaningful reduction in its billing determinant. The result is not merely a weaker incentive; for a customer whose transmission bill is fully pinned to the minimum, the incremental transmission-cost benefit of 12CP response can fall to zero.
That is directly at odds with ERCOT's reliability framework. ERCOT identifies Emergency Response Service (ERS), Load Resource participation, and Voluntary Load Response as demand-response pathways, and ERCOT has expressly observed that customers curtailing in anticipation of 4CP intervals increase reliability by reducing stress on the transmission grid when it is needed most. [4] A transition to 12CP should broaden the coincident-peak signal across the year, not erase the value of responding to it through a separate billing floor.
TBC recognizes that ERS and some ancillary-service participation can provide separate program compensation. That does not make the transmission-price signal irrelevant. Transmission-cost avoidance is a distinct economic layer that can be combined with ERS payments, market-price response, automated curtailment, storage, and other flexibility investments. Removing that layer can eliminate the business case at the margin for voluntary or discretionary participation. The Commission should not assume that flexible loads will continue to provide the same reliability value after the rate design removes the financial reward for reducing transmission use during the very intervals the Commission has selected to measure system contribution.
The Commission can protect other customer classes without choosing a 100% take-or-pay floor. A July 30, 2026 analysis prepared by J. Pollock, Inc. for the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance modeled several minimum-demand levels under a 12CP framework. Under that study's assumptions, an 80% minimum slightly reduced rates for existing customers, while a 75% minimum was rate-neutral; the study's sample residential analysis likewise found that 75% and higher were at or below its no-new-large-load baseline. [3] TBC does not offer that modeling as proof that any minimum is required, and it does not endorse 75% or 80% as the correct answer. The relevant point is that neither 85% nor 100% should be treated as a presumptive floor. Any fallback must preserve a material portion of the bill that remains responsive to actual net 12CP performance.
Most importantly, the finalized interconnection framework already contains multiple tools aimed at the same stranded-cost and abandonment risks. Large-load customers must post financial security, pay cash contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) for specified interconnection costs, pay interconnection fees, enter into long-term interconnection agreements, satisfy financial commitments to reserve capacity, and face capacity-reallocation consequences. Proposed §25.192 also requires interconnection-fee revenue and forfeited financial security to offset TSP transmission revenue requirements. [1] The Commission should evaluate those protections as a coordinated portfolio and avoid imposing multiple mechanisms that recover the same risk or cost.
III.  A Cost-Causation Framework Better Addresses Customer-Specific Risk
TBC does not contend that large loads should be insulated from costs they uniquely cause. If a facility requires a radial line, dedicated substation work, or another facility that is uniquely, demonstrably, and incrementally required to interconnect or expand that customer, direct assignment or cash CIAC can be appropriate. If an existing limited-withdrawal facility later requests additional firm grid service, the newly requested firm MW should be added to the facility's contractual firm-withdrawal base, and the customer should bear customer-specific interconnection costs caused by that incremental request.
The same principle cuts the other direction. A broader network project should not be assigned in full to one large load when it also resolves preexisting reliability violations, replaces aging equipment, serves organic residential or commercial growth, relieves congestion, improves transfer capability or resiliency, supports generation interconnection, or otherwise benefits customers beyond the interconnecting load. The analysis should distinguish customer-specific facilities from systemwide or regional facilities and should account for amounts already recovered through CIAC, interconnection fees, financial security, exit obligations, or capacity subsequently reallocated to other users.
Risk also changes over time. The stranded-cost concern is strongest before energization and during an initial ramp. It is materially different after a facility has energized, completed its ramp, demonstrated creditworthiness and sustained operation, complied with its withdrawal limits, and paid for customer-specific facilities. TBC's primary recommendation is to eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission nevertheless retains a minimum, the mechanism should decline as the underlying exposure declines rather than remain fixed at 100% of gross contracted demand for two decades.
IV.  Responses to the Commission's Specific Questions
Question 1
Should minimum billing-demand values differ for large-load customers with different contracted peak demands or different NCP demands?
Eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission retains one, do not create arbitrary MW tiers based solely on customer size or computational classification; any differentiation should be based on measurable service, cost, and risk characteristics, with the billing determinant anchored to firm net grid withdrawal and actual transmission use.
A customer's gross size is an incomplete proxy for transmission cost causation. A larger project that self-supplies a material portion of its demand and accepts an enforceable firm-withdrawal limit may impose less firm transmission obligation than a smaller project that is fully firm and inflexible. If the Commission retains a minimum, relevant characteristics include contracted firm net grid withdrawal, actual net NCP and net 12CP demand, firm versus non-firm service, controllability, qualified co-located generation and storage, customer-specific transmission costs, project-development risk, and credit or abandonment risk.
Security, direct assignment, and exit obligations may appropriately scale with demonstrated customer-specific cost exposure. The transmission billing determinant, however, should not become a generic penalty for crossing a particular MW threshold. TBC's preferred rule is a common 12CP framework in which similarly situated customers are measured by the same settlement-quality net-withdrawal principle.
Question 2
Should the large-load minimum billing demand be fixed for 20 years, reduced in phases over 20 years, or extended to a longer period?
Eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission nevertheless retains one, do not impose a fixed 20-year minimum on already energized facilities and do not extend any minimum beyond 20 years. Grandfather existing energized loads from the new minimum; at a minimum, materially shorten and phase down any legacy obligation so customers transition toward actual net 12CP as stranded-cost exposure declines.
A fixed 20-year obligation fails to distinguish a speculative project that never energizes from an operating facility that has completed construction, complied with its withdrawal limit, paid customer-specific costs, established a payment history, and demonstrated reliable operations. More fundamentally, an already energized facility made siting, financing, equipment, controls, staffing, co-location, and curtailment decisions under the economic structure in place when it invested. A new facility can price a newly announced billing obligation into its power strategy and capital plan before it commits. A legacy facility cannot retroactively redesign years of sunk investment around a 20-year take-or-pay charge it was never asked to underwrite.
Grandfathering is also a reliability issue. Existing flexible facilities are the loads most likely to have already built the controls, telemetry, operating procedures, storage, self-supply, or curtailment capability that make peak response possible. Imposing a new floor that removes the transmission savings associated with those investments risks testing, on sunk assets, whether Texas can remove a major flexibility incentive without losing some of the flexibility the grid currently receives. TBC sees no reason to run that experiment on already energized facilities when prospective facilities can instead be given clear rules before they invest.
The AEP Ohio experience is instructive on the importance of retaining a coincident-peak transmission signal. In 2024, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio approved AEP Ohio's ESP V for June 2024 through May 2028, including continuation and expansion of its Transmission 1CP (BTCR 1CP pilot), and the Commission separately directed further review of the Rider BTCR pilot's actual results. [5] In Ohio data-center access to 1CP/6CP-style transmission programs advances cost causation because the customer's transmission charge moves with its contribution during the relevant PJM coincident-peak interval or intervals. Ohio's market design is not ERCOT's, but the economic principle is the same: a coincident-peak method works because a customer has something meaningful to gain by reducing load at the system-relevant peak. Texas should not preserve 12CP in name while eliminating that incentive for legacy facilities through a fixed 20-year floor.
TBC's position is therefore: (1) eliminate the minimum; (2) grandfather already energized facilities; (3) if grandfathering is rejected, apply only a short and declining legacy ratchet tied to contracted firm net grid withdrawal, not gross campus demand; (4) for new facilities, use at most a limited performance-sensitive model known before investment; and (5) transition to actual net 12CP as the customer energizes, completes its ramp, and establishes an operating history.
Question 3
If a minimum billing demand is retained, should it use a lower ratchet or a weighted average, and should the contracted-demand component decline over time?
Eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission insists on retaining a fallback, reject a high fixed floor - including an 85% or 100% ratchet - that leaves too little of the bill responsive to customer behavior. Any fallback should use settlement-quality net withdrawal at the POI, preserve a substantial actual-performance component, and decline over time. The Commission should model lower-ratchet and blended alternatives, including a 50% net 12CP / 50% net NCP scenario, rather than presume a high contracted-demand floor.
The problem with an 85% or 100% floor is straightforward: the higher the floor, the smaller the portion of the transmission bill that a customer can influence by curtailing, discharging storage, operating co-located generation, or participating in other flexibility programs. At a sufficiently high floor, a customer can reduce net withdrawal during every 12CP interval and receive little or no transmission-bill benefit. That devalues exactly the behavior ERCOT has recognized as reducing stress on the transmission grid. [4] A fallback designed to protect cost recovery should not simultaneously eliminate the price signal that supports reliability.
A 50% net 12CP / 50% net NCP blend is one fallback scenario worth testing because it attempts to balance two different concepts. The net 12CP component tracks the customer's measured contribution during the system's monthly coincident peaks and preserves a direct incentive to reduce load when the shared transmission system is most stressed. The net NCP component reflects the customer's own highest measured grid withdrawal and can serve as a proxy for the scale of firm service the customer may call upon. A 50/50 blend would therefore leave at least half of the determinant directly sensitive to coincident-peak performance instead of pinning the bill to a high contracted-demand floor.
TBC does not recommend 50/50 as superior to settlement-quality net 12CP, and NCP should not become a backdoor minimum. NCP can occur when the ERCOT system is not near a coincident peak, so it is an imperfect measure of the shared transmission costs that 12CP is intended to allocate. If the Commission evaluates a blend, both CP and NCP must be measured as settlement-quality net grid withdrawal at the POI; gross campus load, nameplate demand, and unconstrained contracted capacity should not be substituted. The Commission should compare a 50/50 case with more CP-weighted cases and lower ratchets, quantify the remaining demand-response incentive under each, and phase down any non-performance component as project risk declines. The July 30 TEBA/JPI modeling further confirms that the record should test lower percentages rather than assume an 85% or 100% floor. [3]
Question 4
Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, such as a data center or cryptocurrency mining facility?
No. Consistent with TBC's longstanding position, the Commission should not create a separate or differential rate class solely because a customer is a data center, cryptocurrency-mining facility, or other computational load. Apply the same cost-causation principles to similarly situated customers and base any differentiation on objective service, operating, and risk characteristics rather than industry identity.
PURA §36.003 requires the Commission to ensure that each rate is just and reasonable. It further provides that a rate may not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory, and must be sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer. [6] TBC does not contend that every classification is unlawful; different treatment can be justified when the record demonstrates a meaningful difference in cost, service, or risk. But computational end use is not itself a measure of transmission cost causation, and it should not be used as a shortcut when actual metering, contracts, controllability, withdrawal limits, and customer-specific facilities are available.
The Commission should instead consider objective factors such as firm versus non-firm service, contracted firm net grid withdrawal, actual net 12CP and NCP demand, load factor, curtailment capability, on-site generation and storage, ramp characteristics, customer-specific facilities, and credit or abandonment risk. A computational facility should remain responsible for the costs and reliability impacts it causes, while receiving the same recognition as other loads for enforceable withdrawal limits, qualified co-located generation, storage, curtailment, non-firm service, and actual net transmission use.
Question 5
Should the definition of transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?
Do not turn the large-load class into a catch-all payer for transmission buildout. Direct assignment should apply only to a project or separable component that is uniquely, demonstrably, incrementally, and not otherwise recovered as a cost of the specific customer or defined customer group. The Commission must evaluate the full stack of CIAC, interconnection costs, financial security, PGRR145 commitments, and proposed SB 6 §25.194 obligations before imposing any additional charge, and it must prevent double recovery.
Large loads already bear material customer-specific interconnection obligations, and the regulatory stack is becoming more substantial. ERCOT's PGRR145/NPRR1325 Batch Zero process became effective July 11, 2026. Separately, the Commission's currently proposed SB 6 rule, new §25.194 in Project No. 58481, would require substantial per-MW financial security before study, a nonrefundable per-MW interconnection fee after study, CIAC for direct interconnection costs, and financial security for system upgrades, with forfeiture and capacity-reallocation consequences for specified withdrawals or milestone failures. [7] Those mechanisms are designed to make large loads financially accountable for the capacity and customer-specific infrastructure they cause.
That accountability cannot run only one direction. Batch-study identification does not establish that every dollar of a recommended network upgrade was caused by one large load. The Commission should require a strict cost-causation analysis that separates facilities required solely to physically interconnect or expand the customer from regional facilities that also remedy preexisting reliability needs, replace aging infrastructure, serve organic load growth, reduce congestion, improve transfer capability or resiliency, support generation, or benefit other users. A large load should not become the funding source for a broader transmission project merely because its interconnection study provided the occasion to identify that project.
Any additional assignment must also credit CIAC and customer-specific interconnection costs already paid, financial security or forfeited security, interconnection fees, exit payments, and any value associated with capacity later released or reallocated. Otherwise, the Commission risks creating customer-side stranded investment: a developer can pay to reserve capacity, secure upgrades, and build a facility, only to be charged again for regional projects that serve other rate classes as well. That is not cost causation; it is cost aggregation. It can also make Texas less competitive for capital-intensive projects by converting the large-load classification into an open-ended source of transmission revenue without a project-specific causal showing.
Question 6
If a large-load customer can reserve transmission capacity before energizing or fully using that capacity, how should those loads be reflected in resource-adequacy reports, assessments, and transmission-planning studies?
Monitor and report reserved-but-unused capacity, but do not make reporting itself a new trigger to confiscate or reallocate capacity that a customer has paid for, secured, and been contractually promised. Once a customer has satisfied applicable financial, contractual, and development milestones for firm MW, that committed capacity should remain with the customer unless the customer voluntarily releases it or an existing, clearly defined contractual or regulatory trigger authorizes reallocation. Planning should clearly distinguish committed-but-not-yet-used MW from speculative or forfeitable MW.
Reserved capacity is relevant to planning, but 'unused' does not mean 'uncommitted.' Planning reports should distinguish among gross internal or nameplate demand, contracted firm net grid withdrawal, any WLPUN withdrawal limit, qualified co-located generation, storage, controllable or curtailable demand, energized and observed demand, reserved-but-not-yet-energized capacity, expected ramp schedule, development milestones, probability of completion, and exposure if co-located generation or storage is unavailable. This reporting can improve the planning record without altering the customer's contractual entitlement to capacity.
For resource adequacy, ERCOT should use project-maturity milestones and probability-weighted scenarios rather than treating every requested MW as equally certain. For transmission planning, ERCOT should study normal expected net withdrawal, maximum enforceable firm withdrawal, credible generator or storage outages, contingency conditions, contractually required curtailment, expected project ramp, and reasonable high- and low-load sensitivities. Billing, resource adequacy, and transmission planning need not use one identical number. Planning can evaluate conservative contingencies without billing the customer every month as if the worst-case contingency occurs continuously.
The same distinction should govern reallocation. If a customer has posted required security, paid required amounts, met its milestones, and holds a binding commitment for specified firm MW, ERCOT or a TSP should not reassign those MW solely because current observed usage is temporarily below the reservation. Reallocation may be appropriate where a customer voluntarily releases capacity, fails a clearly defined milestone, withdraws under the governing agreement, or otherwise triggers an established forfeiture provision. But a planning report should not create a new and independent reallocation authority. Otherwise, the original customer can remain financially responsible for capacity while another project receives the benefit, which turns cost causation on its head.
ERCOT and the Commission should also consider a load-side analogue to Southwest Power Pool's Hosting Capacity Tool. Section 3.1.2.1 of SPP's Consolidated Planning Process Manual describes a public pre-screening tool that is updated after cluster studies or restudies and evaluates potential interconnection amounts at individual POIs under N-0 and N-1 conditions, with outputs including distribution factors, MW impacts, and transmission-facility loading before and after a proposed injection. [8] SPP's tool is designed for generator interconnection, and the CPP Manual notes that portions of the underlying framework remain pending FERC approval, so it is not a direct template for ERCOT load. But the concept is useful: a transparent POI-level hosting-capacity and regional-impact tool for load could help ERCOT distinguish physical headroom, capacity already committed to projects, and the incremental system impact of additional MW before deciding whether capacity is available for another project or which customer class caused a particular upgrade.
V.  Recommendations
TBC respectfully requests that the Commission:
Adopt the transition to 12CP while retaining Commission- and ERCOT-selected monthly 30-minute system-peak intervals and measuring each large-load customer's contribution using settlement-quality net grid withdrawal at the POI.
Delete the proposed large-load minimum billing demand and apply the ordinary 12CP methodology to large-load customers, preserving the transmission-price signal that rewards actual reductions in net grid withdrawal during system peaks.
Recognize enforceable WLPUN withdrawal limits, qualified BYOG and co-located generation, storage, controllability, curtailment, and non-firm service to the extent they reduce the customer's firm grid-withdrawal obligation or actual net 12CP demand.
If a minimum billing demand is retained, grandfather already energized facilities. If the Commission rejects grandfathering, use only a short, declining legacy mechanism based on contracted firm net grid withdrawal. For prospective facilities, preserve a substantial actual-performance component and model lower-ratchet or blended alternatives - including a 50% net 12CP / 50% net NCP scenario and more CP-weighted cases - rather than adopting an 85% or 100% floor.
Reject separate rate treatment based solely on a Large Computational Load classification and instead apply objective cost, service, and risk characteristics consistently across similarly situated customers.
Directly assign interconnection and batch-study costs only where they are uniquely, demonstrably, incrementally, and not otherwise recovered as costs caused by the customer or a defined customer group. Account for CIAC, interconnection fees, security, PGRR145 commitments, proposed §25.194 obligations, and other recoveries; do not use the large-load class as a catch-all for multi-beneficiary regional upgrades.
Require resource-adequacy and transmission-planning reports to identify reserved-but-unused capacity, project maturity, ramp, expected net withdrawal, and maximum enforceable firm withdrawal, while protecting firm MW that a customer has paid for, secured, and contractually retained absent a defined release or forfeiture trigger. Direct ERCOT to evaluate a transparent, load-side POI hosting-capacity tool modeled conceptually on SPP's pre-screening approach.
TBC and its members remain committed to working with the Commission, ERCOT, utilities, consumer representatives, and other stakeholders on a transmission framework that protects existing customers while preserving the incentives for large loads to reduce grid dependence and respond when the system needs flexibility. A 12CP methodology based on settlement-quality net grid withdrawal accomplishes that objective more directly than a 20-year minimum billing demand based on contracted capacity. Texas should not adopt a coincident-peak methodology and then remove the economic consequence of responding to the coincident peaks.
Respectfully submitted,
TEXAS BLOCKCHAIN COUNCIL

Director of Policy & Technology

I. TBC Supports 12CP With Settlement-Quality Net Grid Withdrawal at the
Point of Interconnection

customer's billing demand be the settlement-quality net import from the transmission system at

                            Applicable ERCOT Monthly Peak Interval

subtract every generator, storage device, or individual load located behind the meter. It can use
the amount that the customer actually withdrew from the ERCOT transmission system during

limit at a single POI determined through a system-wide interconnection study. [2] That
enforceable withdrawal limit - not the gross internal demand of every load behind the POI - is
the relevant measure of the firm transmission service the grid has committed to provide. A
campus with 1,000 MW of internal demand but an enforceable 400 MW maximum grid-
withdrawal limit is not receiving 1,000 MW of firm transmission service.

TBC recommends the same functional treatment for qualified BYOG arrangements, co-located
generation, and energy storage. The credit should not be based merely on nameplate capacity.
It should be tied to settlement-quality metering and telemetry, applicable interconnection and
planning studies, operational availability, enforceable operating requirements, and a contractual
or physical limitation on the customer's entitlement to withdraw above its established firm limit.
Likewise, controllable and non-firm loads should not be billed as though every MW were
continuously entitled to firm service when the customer has accepted enforceable curtailment
or withdrawal restrictions.

Il. The Proposed 20-Year Minimum Billing Demand Should Be Rejected
The minimum billing demand is not necessary to implement 12CP. It is a separate overlaythat
would adjust a large load's measured 12CP upward whenever contracted peak demand or
annual NCP is higher. Proposed §25.252 would also require a large-load interconnection
agreement with a term of at least 20 years, while proposed §25.193 and §25.252 would cause
billing to begin when transmission capacity is made available and would require 240 consecutive
monthly payments during the first 20 years based on the greater of contracted peak demand,
prior-year NCP, or 12CP demand. [1]

That approach can disconnect a substantial portion of the transmission bill from the customer's
actual contribution during the 12 monthly peaks. A customer that invests in on-site generation,
storage, automated load controls, or a WLPUN structure may reduce its actual grid withdrawal
and provide measurable system value, yet receive little or no transmission-cost recognition if it
remains billed at its original contracted peak. A flexible load may curtail at every monthly system
peak and still see no meaningful reduction in its billing determinant. The result is not merely a
weaker incentive; for a customer whose transmission bill is fully pinned to the minimum, the
incremental transmission-cost benefit of 12CP response can fall to zero.

That is directly at odds with ERCOT's reliability framework. ERCOT identifies Emergency
Response Service (ERS), Load Resource participation, and Voluntary Load Response as demand-
response pathways, and ERCOT has expressly observed that customers curtailing in anticipation
of 4CP intervals increase reliability by reducing stress on the transmission grid when it is needed
most. [4] A transition to 12CP should broaden the coincident-peak signal across the year, not
erase the value of responding to it through a separate billing floor.

TBC recognizes that ERS and some ancillary-service participation can provide separate program
compensation. That does not make the transmission-price signal irrelevant. Transmission-cost
avoidance is a distinct economic layer that can be combined with ERS payments, market-price
response, automated curtailment, storage, and other flexibility investments. Removing that
layer can eliminate the business case at the margin for voluntary or discretionary participation.
The Commission should not assume that flexible loads will continue to provide the same
reliability value after the rate design removes the financial reward for reducing transmission use
during the very intervals the Commission has selected to measure system contribution.

The Commission can protect other customer classes without choosing a 100% take-or-pay floor.
A July 30,2026 analysis prepared by J. Pollock, Inc. for the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance modeled
several minimum-demand levels under a 12CP framework. Under that study's assumptions, an
80% minimum slightly reduced rates for existing customers, while a 75% minimum was rate-
neutral; the study's sample residential analysis likewise found that 75% and higher were at or
below its no-new-large-load baseline. [3] TBC does not offer that modeling as proof that any
minimum is required, and it does not endorse 75% or 80% as the correct answer. The relevant
point is that neither 85% nor 100% should be treated as a presumptive floor. Any fallback must
preserve a material portion of the bill that remains responsive to actual net 12CP performance.

Most importantly, the finalized interconnection framework already contains multiple tools
aimed at the same stranded-cost and abandonment risks. Large-load customers must post
financial security, pay cash contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) for specified
interconnection costs, pay interconnection fees, enter into long-term interconnection
agreements, satisfy financial commitments to reserve capacity, and face capacity-reallocation
consequences. Proposed §25.192 also requires interconnection-fee revenue and forfeited
financial security to offset TSP transmission revenue requirements. [1] The Commission should
evaluate those protections as a coordinated portfolio and avoid imposing multiple mechanisms
that recover the same risk or cost.

Ill. A Cost-Causation Framework Better Addresses Customer-Specific Risk
TBC does not contend that large loads should be insulated from costs they uniquely cause. If a
facility requires a radial line, dedicated substation work, or another facility that is uniquely,
demonstrably, and incrementally required to interconnect or expand that customer, direct
assignment or cash CIAC can be appropriate. If an existing limited-withdrawal facility later
requests additional firm grid service, the newly requested firm MW should be added to the
facility's contractual firm-withdrawal base, and the customer should bear customer-specific
interconnection costs caused by that incremental request.

The same principle cuts the other direction. A broader network project should not be assigned
in full to one large load when it also resolves preexisting reliability violations, replaces aging
equipment, serves organic residential or commercial growth, relieves congestion, improves
transfer capability or resiliency, supports generation interconnection, or otherwise benefits
customers beyond the interconnecting load. The analysis should distinguish customer-specific
facilities from systemwide or regional facilities and should account for amounts already
recovered through CIAC, interconnection fees, financial security, exit obligations, or capacity
subsequently reallocated to other users.

Risk also changes over time. The stranded-cost concern is strongest before energization and
during an initial ramp. It is materially different after a facility has energized, completed its ramp,
demonstrated creditworthiness and sustained operation, complied with its withdrawal limits,
and paid for customer-specific facilities. TBC's primary recommendation is to eliminate the
minimum billing demand. If the Commission nevertheless retains a minimum, the mechanism
should decline as the underlying exposure declines rather than remain fixed at 100% of gross
contracted demand for two decades.

IV. Responses to the Commission's Specific Questions

Question 1
Should minimum billing-demand values differ for large-load customers with different contracted
peakdemands ordifferent NCP demands?

Eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission retains one, do not create arbitrary
MW tiers based solely on customer size or computational classification; any differentiation
should be based on measurable service, cost, and risk characteristics, with the billing
determinant anchored to firm net grid withdrawal and actual transmission use.
A customer's gross size is an incomplete proxy for transmission cost causation. A larger project
that self-supplies a material portion of its demand and accepts an enforceable firm-withdrawal
limit may impose less firm transmission obligation than a smaller project that is fully firm and
inflexible. If the Commission retains a minimum, relevant characteristics include contracted firm
net grid withdrawal, actual net NCP and net 12CP demand, firm versus non-firm service,
controllability, qualified co-located generation and storage, customer-specific transmission
costs, project-development risk, and credit or abandonment risk.

Security, direct assignment, and exit obligations may appropriately scale with demonstrated
customer-specific cost exposure. The transmission billing determinant, however, should not
become a generic penalty for crossing a particular MW threshold. TBC's preferred rule is a
common 12CP framework in which similarly situated customers are measured by the same
settlement-quality net-withdrawal principle.

Question 2
Should the large-load minimum billing demand be fixed for 20 years, reduced in phases over 20
years, or extended to a longer period?
Eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission nevertheless retains one, do not
impose a fixed 20-year minimum on already energized facilities and do not extend any
minimum beyond 20 years. Grandfather existing energized loads from the new minimum; at a
minimum, materially shorten and phase down any legacy obligation so customers transition
toward actual net 12CP as stranded-cost exposure declines.

A fixed 20-year obligation fails to distinguish a speculative project that never energizes from an
operating facility that has completed construction, complied with its withdrawal limit, paid
customer-specific costs, established a payment history, and demonstrated reliable operations.
More fundamentally, an already energized facility made siting, financing, equipment, controls,
staffing, co-location, and curtailment decisions under the economic structure in place when it
invested. A new facility can price a newly announced billing obligation into its power strategy
and capital plan before it commits. A legacy facility cannot retroactively redesign years of sunk
investment around a 20-year take-or-pay charge it was never asked to underwrite.

Grandfathering is also a reliability issue. Existing flexible facilities are the loads most likely to
have already built the controls, telemetry, operating procedures, storage, self-supply, or
curtailment capability that make peak response possible. Imposing a new floor that removes the
transmission savings associated with those investments risks testing, on sunk assets, whether
Texas can remove a major flexibility incentive without losing some of the flexibility the grid
currently receives. TBC sees no reason to run that experiment on already energized facilities
when prospective facilities can instead be given clear rules before they invest.

The AEP Ohio experience is instructive on the importance of retaining a coincident-peak
transmission signal. In 2024, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio approved AEP Ohio's ESP V
for June 2024 through May 2028, including continuation and expansion of its Transmission 1CP
(BTCR 1CP pilot), and the Commission separately directed further review of the Rider BTCR
pilot's actual results. [5] In Ohio data-center access to 1CP/6CP-style transmission programs
advances cost causation because the customer's transmission charge moves with its
contribution during the relevant PJM coincident-peak interval or intervals. Ohio's market design
is not ERCOT's, but the economic principle is the same: a coincident-peak method works
because a customer has something meaningful to gain by reducing load at the system-relevant
peak. Texas should not preserve 12CP in name while eliminating that incentive for legacy
facilities through a fixed 20-year floor.

TBC's position is therefore: (1) eliminate the minimum; (2) grandfather already energized
facilities; (3) if grandfathering is rejected, apply only a short and declining legacy ratchet tied to
contracted firm net grid withdrawal, not gross campus demand; (4) for new facilities, use at
most a limited performance-sensitive model known before investment; and (5) transition to
actual net 12CP as the customer energizes, completes its ramp, and establishes an operating
history.

Question 3
If a minimum billing demand is retained, should it use a lower ratchet or a weighted average,
and should the contracted-demand component decline overtime?
Eliminate the minimum billing demand. If the Commission insists on retaining a fallback, reject
a high fixed floor - including an 85% or 100% ratchet - that leaves too little of the bill
responsive to customer behavior. Any fallback should use settlement-quality net withdrawal
at the POI, preserve a substantial actual-performance component, and decline over time. The
Commission should model lower-ratchet and blended alternatives, including a 50% net 12CP /
50% net NCP scenario, rather than presume a high contracted-demand floor.

The problem with an 85% or 100% floor is straightforward: the higher the floor, the smallerthe
portion of the transmission bill that a customer can influence by curtailing, discharging storage,
operating co-located generation, or participating in other flexibility programs. At a sufficiently
high floor, a customer can reduce net withdrawal during every 12CP interval and receive little or
no transmission-bill benefit. That devalues exactly the behavior ERCOT has recognized as

reducing stress on the transmission grid. [4] A fallback designed to protect cost recovery should
not simultaneously eliminatethe price signal that supports reliability.

A 50% net 12CP / 50% net NCP blend is one fallback scenario worth testing because it attempts
to balance two different concepts. The net 12CP component tracks the customer's measured
contribution during the system's monthly coincident peaks and preserves a direct incentive to
reduce load when the shared transmission system is most stressed. The net NCP component
reflects the customer's own highest measured grid withdrawal and can serve as a proxy for the
scale of firm service the customer may call upon. A 50/50 blend would therefore leave at least
half of the determinant directly sensitive to coincident-peak performance instead of pinning the
bill to a high contracted-demand floor.

TBC does not recommend 50/50 as superior to settlement-quality net 12CP, and NCP should not
become a backdoor minimum. NCP can occur when the ERCOT system is not near a coincident
peak, so it is an imperfect measure of the shared transmission costs that 12CP is intended to
allocate. If the Commission evaluates a blend, both CP and NCP must be measured as
settlement-quality net grid withdrawal at the POI; gross campus load, nameplate demand, and
unconstrained contracted capacity should not be substituted. The Commission should compare
a 50/50 case with more CP-weighted cases and lower ratchets, quantify the remaining demand-
response incentive under each, and phase down any non-performance component as project
risk declines. The July 30 TEBA/JPI modeling further confirms that the record should test lower
percentages rather than assume an 85% or 100% floor. [3]

Question 4
Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, such as a data center
or cryptocurrency mining facility?
No. Consistent with TBC's longstanding position, the Commission should not create a separate
or differential rate class solely because a customer is a data center, cryptocurrency-mining
facility, or other computational load. Apply the same cost-causation principles to similarly
situated customers and base any differentiation on objective service, operating, and risk
characteristics rather than industry identity.
PURA §36.003 requires the Commission to ensure that each rate is just and reasonable. It
further provides that a rate may not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory,
and must be sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer. [6]
TBC does not contend that every classification is unlawful; different treatment can be justified
when the record demonstrates a meaningful difference in cost, service, or risk. But
computational end use is not itself a measure of transmission cost causation, and it should not
be used as a shortcut when actual metering, contracts, controllability, withdrawal limits, and
customer-specific facilities are available.

The Commission should instead consider objective factors such as firm versus non-firm service,
contracted firm net grid withdrawal, actual net 12CP and NCP demand, load factor, curtailment
capability, on-site generation and storage, ramp characteristics, customer-specific facilities, and

credit or abandonment risk. A computational facility should remain responsible for the costs and
reliability impacts it causes, while receiving the same recognition as other loads for enforceable
withdrawal limits, qualified co-located generation, storage, curtailment, non-firm service, and
actual net transmission use.

Question 5
Should the definition Of transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include transmission
projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity
needs Of a particular load?

Do not turn the large-load class into a catch-all payer for transmission buildout. Direct
assignment should apply only to a project or separable component that is uniquely,
demonstrably, incrementally, and not otherwise recovered as a cost of the specific customer
or defined customer group. The Commission must evaluate the full stack of CIAC,
interconnection costs, financial security, PGRR145 commitments, and proposed SB 6 §25.194
obligations before imposing any additional charge, and it must prevent double recovery.
Large loads already bear material customer-specific interconnection obligations, and the
regulatory stack is becoming more substantial. ERCOT's PGRR145/NPRR1325 Batch Zero process
became effective July 11, 2026. Separately, the Commission's currently proposed SB 6 rule, new
§25.194 in Project No. 58481, would require substantial per-MW financial security before study,
a nonrefundable per-MW interconnection fee after study, CIAC for direct interconnection costs,
and financial security for system upgrades, with forfeiture and capacity-reallocation
consequences for specified withdrawals or milestone failures. [7] Those mechanisms are
designed to make large loads financially accountable for the capacity and customer-specific
infrastructure they cause.

That accountability cannot run only one direction. Batch-study identification does not establish
that every dollar of a recommended network upgrade was caused by one large load. The
Commission should require a strict cost-causation analysis that separates facilities required
solelyto physically interconnect or expand the customer from regional facilities that also
remedy preexisting reliability needs, replace aging infrastructure, serve organic load growth,
reduce congestion, improve transfer capability or resiliency, support generation, or benefit
other users. A large load should not become the funding source for a broader transmission
project merely because its interconnection study provided the occasion to identify that project.
Any additional assignment must also credit CIAC and customer-specific interconnection costs
already paid, financial security or forfeited security, interconnection fees, exit payments, and
any value associated with capacity later released or reallocated. Otherwise, the Commission
risks creating customer-side stranded investment: a developer can pay to reserve capacity,
secure upgrades, and build a facility, only to be charged again for regional projects that serve
other rate classes as well. That is not cost causation; it is cost aggregation. It can also make
Texas less competitive for capital-intensive projects by converting the large-load classification
into an open-ended source of transmission revenue without a project-specific causal showing.

Question 6
If a large-load customer can reserve transmission capacity before energizing or fully using that
capacity, how should those loads be reflected in resource-adequacy reports, assessments, and
transmission-planning studies?
Monitor and report reserved-but-unused capacity, but do not make reporting itself a new
trigger to confiscate or reallocate capacity that a customer has paid for, secured, and been
contractually promised. Once a customer has satisfied applicable financial, contractual, and
development milestones for firm MW, that committed capacity should remain with the
customer unless the customer voluntarily releases it or an existing, clearly defined contractual
or regulatory trigger authorizes reallocation. Planning should clearly distinguish committed-
but-not-yet-used MW from speculative or forfeitable MW.

Reserved capacity is relevant to planning, but 'unused' does not mean 'uncommitted.' Planning
reports should distinguish among gross internal or nameplate demand, contracted firm net grid
withdrawal, any WLPUN withdrawal limit, qualified co-located generation, storage, controllable
or curtailable demand, energized and observed demand, reserved-but-not-yet-energized
capacity, expected ramp schedule, development milestones, probability of completion, and
exposure if co-located generation or storage is unavailable. This reporting can improve the
planning record without altering the customer's contractual entitlementto capacity.

For resource adequacy, ERCOT should use project-maturity milestones and probability-weighted
scenarios rather than treating every requested MW as equally certain. For transmission
planning, ERCOT should study normal expected net withdrawal, maximum enforceable firm
withdrawal, credible generator or storage outages, contingency conditions, contractually
required curtailment, expected project ramp, and reasonable high- and low-load sensitivities.
Billing, resource adequacy, and transmission planning need not use one identical number.
Planning can evaluate conservative contingencies without billing the customer every month as if
the worst-case contingency occurs continuously.

The same distinction should govern reallocation. If a customer has posted required security,
paid required amounts, met its milestones, and holds a binding commitment for specified firm
MW, ERCOT or a TSP should not reassign those MW solely because current observed usage is
temporarily below the reservation. Reallocation may be appropriate where a customer
voluntarily releases capacity, fails a clearly defined milestone, withdraws under the governing
agreement, or otherwise triggers an established forfeiture provision. But a planning report
should not create a new and independent reallocation authority. Otherwise, the original
customer can remain financially responsible for capacity while another project receives the
benefit, which turns cost causation on its head.

ERCOT and the Commission should also consider a load-side analogue to Southwest Power
Pool's Hosting Capacity Tool. Section 3.1.2.1 of SPP's Consolidated Planning Process Manual
describes a public pre-screening tool that is updated after cluster studies or restudies and
evaluates potential interconnection amounts at individual POIs under N-0 and N-1 conditions,
with outputs including distribution factors, MW impacts, and transmission-facility loading before

V. Recommendations
TBC respectfully requests that the Commission:

1.   Adopt the transition to 12CP while retaining Commission- and ERCOT-selected monthly 30-
     minute system-peak intervals and measuring each large-load customer's contribution using
     settlement-quality net grid withdrawal at the POI.
2.   Delete the proposed large-load minimum billing demand and applythe ordinary 12CP
     methodology to large-load customers, preserving the transmission-price signal that rewards
     actual reductions in net grid withdrawal during system peaks.
3.   Recognize enforceable WLPUN withdrawal limits, qualified BYOG and co-located generation,
     storage, controllability, curtailment, and non-firm service to the extent they reduce the
     customer's firm grid-withdrawal obligation or actual net 12CP demand.
4.   If a minimum billing demand is retained, grandfather already energized facilities. If the
     Commission rejects grandfathering, use only a short, declining legacy mechanism based on
     contracted firm net grid withdrawal. For prospective facilities, preserve a substantial actual-
     performance component and model lower-ratchet or blended alternatives - including a 50%
     net 12CP / 50% net NCP scenario and more CP-weighted cases - rather than adopting an
     85% or 100% floor.
5.   Reject separate rate treatment based solely on a Large Computational Load classification
     and instead apply objective cost, service, and risk characteristics consistently across similarly
     situated customers.
6.   Directly assign interconnection and batch-study costs only where they are uniquely,
     demonstrably, incrementally, and not otherwise recovered as costs caused by the customer
     or a defined customer group. Account for CIAC, interconnection fees, security, PGRR145
     commitments, proposed §25.194 obligations, and other recoveries; do not use the large-
     load class as a catch-all for multi-beneficiary regional upgrades.
7.   Require resource-adequacy and transmission-planning reports to identify reserved-but-
     unused capacity, project maturity, ramp, expected net withdrawal, and maximum
     enforceable firm withdrawal, while protecting firm MW that a customer has paid for,
     secured, and contractually retained absent a defined release or forfeiture trigger. Direct
     ERCOT to evaluate a transparent, load-side POI hosting-capacity tool modeled conceptually
     on SPP's pre-screening approach.

TBC and its members remain committed to working with the Commission, ERCOT, utilities,
consumer representatives, and other stakeholders on a transmission framework that protects
